topics.title: 3.1 An introduction to the role of the accountant in business

outcomes.text: Describe what an accountant is responsible for in a business.
Tell financial accounting from management accounting and state the purpose of each.
Explain how accountants run information systems and oversee bookkeepers and ledger clerks.
Describe sole traders, partnerships, private limited companies and plcs.
Explain the benefits, risks and reporting impact of each ownership model.
Match sources of finance (capital, overdraft, loan, mortgage, shares, debentures) to business types and their risks.

subtopics.title: Source documents and books of prime entry

outcomes.text: Record transactions from source documents such as invoices, credit notes, till rolls and bank statements.
Use the purchases, sales, returns, general journals and three column cash book.
Post to receivables, payables and general ledger accounts.
Handle discounts, disposals of non-current assets, irrecoverable debts and contra entries.
Tell revenue from capital expenditure and income.
Record accruals, prepayments, income due and income received in advance.
Record provisions for doubtful debts, depreciation, disposals and opening/closing inventory.
Prepare and understand accounting records from source documents.
Apply double entry in statements for a range of business organisations.
Prepare income statements and statements of financial position from trial balances for service and trading businesses.
Lay out a statement of financial position with proper subheadings.

subtopics.title: Prepayments, bad debts and depreciation entries

outcomes.text: Make ledger and statement entries for prepayments and accruals.
Make entries for irrecoverable debts and their recovery.
Make entries for straight line and reducing balance depreciation.
Use trial balances, bank reconciliations and sales and purchases ledger control accounts to check records.
Handle contras, overdue interest and unusual balances in control accounts.
Correct double entry errors with the general journal and suspense account.
Show how errors change profit and the statement of financial position, including redrafting statements.
Weigh the benefits and limits of each verification technique.
Identify errors a trial balance reveals: addition, partial omission, transposition, unequal posting.
Identify errors it misses: commission, reversal, compensating, omission, original entry, principle.

topics.title: 3.5 Accounting concepts used in the preparation of accounting records

outcomes.text: State the general accounting concepts such as money measurement, duality, cost, going concern, accruals, consistency, prudence, materiality, realisation and business entity.
Apply concepts to preparing statements, asset valuation, depreciation and inventory valuation at cost or net realisable value.
Apply concepts to recording non-current asset purchases, ledger entries and sale or return goods.

topics.title: 3.6 Preparation of financial statements of sole traders

outcomes.text: Use concepts to record accruals, depreciation, disposals, doubtful debts, drawings in goods, sale or return and inventory.
Prepare sole traders' statements from ledger accounts including adjustments, for service and trading businesses.
Prepare income statements and statements of financial position from a trial balance with adjustments.
Prepare internal income statements for limited companies, separating operating profit, profit before tax and after tax.
Prepare a statement of changes in equity with share issues, premiums, dividends and profit.
Prepare a company statement of financial position with the correct sub-headings.

topics.title: 3.8 Analysis and evaluation of financial information

outcomes.text: Calculate and interpret margin, markup, inventory turnover, profit and expense ratios and return on capital employed.
Calculate and interpret current, liquid capital, receivable days, payable days and gearing ratios.
Appraise performance on profitability, liquidity, efficiency and capital structure.
Explain the difference between cash and profit and how transactions affect each.
Explain the limits of financial statements and ratio analysis, financial and non-financial.
Explain why organisations budget.
Discuss the benefits and limits of budgeting and budgetary control, including zero-based and incremental budgets.
Prepare cash, sales, purchases, production, labour and financial statement budgets.
Explain how budgets are used for planning and control and calculate and interpret variances.
Classify costs as direct, indirect, variable, semi-variable, fixed or stepped.
Define marginal cost, contribution and break-even.
Calculate and interpret break-even points and break-even charts.
Explain the uses and limits of break-even analysis.
Use marginal costing and non-financial factors for make-or-buy, extra work, pricing, scarce resources, closing a line and target profit decisions.
Explain the purpose, advantages and disadvantages of standard costing.
Calculate and interpret materials, labour and sales variances.
Explain how variances relate to each other.
Reconcile budgeted and actual cost or profit.
Use absorption costing to find a product's total cost: allocation, apportionment, overhead absorption rates, under and over absorption.
Use ABC with cost pools and cost drivers to attribute indirect costs to products.
Use absorption and ABC costs to set selling prices.
Compare benefits and limits of absorption, ABC and marginal costing, including inventory valuation and profit effects.
Calculate and use cash flows in investment appraisal.
Calculate the payback period and net present value of a project, using discount factors and cost of capital.
Discuss the benefits and limits of payback and NPV.
Use appraisal measures with financial and non-financial factors to evaluate projects.

topics.title: 3.14 Accounting for organisations with incomplete records

outcomes.text: Calculate profit when records are insufficient, using statements of affairs.
Use control accounts, cash and bank accounts, ratios, depreciation and disposal calculations to find missing figures.
Compare single entry and double entry record keeping.
Prepare and comment on partnership income statements, appropriation accounts and statements of financial position.
Calculate interest on capital and drawings, partner salaries and loan interest, and share profits and losses.
Prepare partners' capital and current accounts, applying the Partnership Act 1890 when there is no agreement.
Account for asset revaluation and goodwill.
Account for a partner's retirement or a new partner's admission.
Draft company statements to IAS1, including cash flow statements by the indirect method (IAS7) and schedules of non-current assets.
Account for revaluation of non-current assets.
Tell share issues, rights issues and bonus issues apart and record their effects in the statements.
Explain why accounts are published, their elements and limits, and how stakeholders use them.
Explain the purpose and importance of the international accounting standards framework.

topics.title: 3.17 Interpretation, analysis and communication of accounting information

outcomes.text: Use techniques and ratios to analyse financial and management information, including investor ratios: dividend yield, EPS, dividend cover, price earnings, interest cover.
Evaluate performance internally across periods and externally against competitors.
Distinguish cash from profit and the effect of transactions on profitability and liquidity.
Explain the interests of internal and external stakeholders and why clear communication matters.
Compare accounting software and computerised with manual systems.
Compare single and double entry systems.
Critically assess recommendations and their impact on stakeholders, the economy and the environment.
State the fundamental principles: integrity, objectivity, competence and care, confidentiality, professional behaviour.
Explain how these principles affect accountants, auditors, directors, governance and social responsibility.
Explain the legal and regulatory frameworks for accounting and the consequences of breaching them.
Explain how professional bodies set and enforce codes of conduct.
Act ethically with clients, suppliers, colleagues and stakeholders, following codes and regulation.
Choose appropriate action on suspected unethical or illegal acts: safeguards, threat evaluation, conflicts of interest, outside advice.
